findings.claim: Syngman Rhee was 'a fiercely anti-communist exile who had spent decades campaigning for independence from the United States'.
findings.truth: Rhee was exiled IN the United States and campaigned for Korean independence FROM Japan. As written the sentence says he wanted independence from America.
findings.evidence: Spec part one names Syngman Rhee; Wikipedia 'Syngman Rhee' (exile in the USA 1912-45, independence movement against Japanese rule).

findings.claim: (lessons 1, 3, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13) 27 of the 78 practice questions use the stem 'Construct a chronological explanation of ...' for the 8-mark question.
findings.truth: The 8-mark question in this section is a narrative account and is set as 'Write an account of ...'. Every stem converted; the mark schemes already described a narrative account and were left alone.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure: the third question of each wider world depth study is 'Write an account...', 8 marks, AO1+AO2.

findings.claim: 'Within hours Truman ordered US air and naval forces to defend the south.'
findings.truth: News reached Truman on the evening of 24 June; air and naval support was authorised at the second Blair House meeting on 26 June and announced on 27 June - about two days, not hours.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Korean War'; the lesson's own Source A is dated 27 June 1950.

findings.claim: Revision tip: 'this is a frequently testable specific detail'.
findings.truth: An invented claim about what the exam tests. Replaced with a neutral prompt.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented exam claims.

findings.claim: 'Avoid drifting into your own knowledge: stay on what the source says' for the 4-mark source question.
findings.truth: The 4-mark source question tests AO3 and explicitly asks the student to explain the answer using the source AND contextual knowledge. The tip trained students to leave out half of what is credited.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B question 1 (source analysis, 4 marks, AO3).

findings.claim: (lessons 2, 6) All twelve 4-mark questions in lessons 2 and 6 use 'Using Source X, identify two reasons ...'.
findings.truth: The 4-mark question asks how you know a source suggests something, answered from the source plus contextual knowledge. Stems and mark schemes rebuilt; a contextual-knowledge line added to each scheme.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B question 1.

findings.claim: 'landing craft put X Corps ashore at three beaches, codenamed Red, Green and Blue' at the evening high tide.
findings.truth: Green Beach was the morning landing on Wolmido. The evening landings were at Red and Blue beaches only.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battle of Inchon' (Green Beach on the northern side of Wolmido; Red in Inchon proper; Blue four miles south-east).

findings.claim: 'examiners reward causal links, not chronology alone'.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; reworded as advice about the question.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented exam claims.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer 'Extreme tides, narrow channels, no beaches and the risk of catastrophic failure.'
findings.truth: A four-item list answer fails the flashcard validator. Replaced with one idea.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: flashcard answers must not be comma lists.

findings.claim: Source H is 'An extract from the official biography of MacArthur by Geoffrey Perret, published in 1996', with an invented quotation.
findings.truth: The quotation is composed, and Perret's 1996 book is not an official biography (MacArthur's authorised biographer was D. Clayton James). The ascription no longer names a real author for words he did not write.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: invented quotations attributed to real named historians are HIGH.

findings.claim: Two flashcard answers are bare lists ('Night attacks, mass infantry assaults, infiltration, no long supply lines, and bugles instead of radios'; 'Bomb China, blockade its coast, deploy Nationalist troops and consider atomic weapons').
findings.truth: Both replaced with single-idea answers.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: no list answers.

findings.claim: (lessons 5, 10, 13) Three exam tips describe the 16-mark question as a 'Source-Based Essay' in which students must integrate the supplied sources; two also cite 'examiner reports'.
findings.truth: The 16-mark question in this section supplies no sources. It quotes a statement and asks how far the student agrees, is marked on AO1+AO2, and is the only question here carrying four SPaG marks. All three tips rewritten, with the SPaG fact stated.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B question 4 (essay requiring a judgement, 8 AO1 + 8 AO2 + 4 SPaG).

findings.claim: 'exactly the kind of comparative judgement examiners reward'.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; reworded.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented exam claims.

findings.claim: 'Most importantly for AQA, the war made the Vietnam War almost inevitable.'
findings.truth: Asserts an exam emphasis and states a contested determinist judgement as fact. Reworded to 'made deeper American involvement in Vietnam far more likely'.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented exam claims; causation stated as probability, not inevitability.

findings.claim: All six practice questions are '16 marks - Source-Based Essay' built on three sources each, including invented quotations ascribed to named living or recently living historians (Bruce Cumings 2010 and 1999, William Stueck 1995, Stephen Bull 2007, Rosemary Foot 1981, James Matray 2003), an invented private letter from a named US soldier, an invented Chinese soldier's diary and an invented inscription at the UN Memorial Cemetery in Busan.
findings.truth: This paper sets no source-based essay. All six converted to the statement essay with rebuilt mark schemes; every invented historian quotation and invented source is retired with them.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B question 4; checker brief on fabricated sources and invented historian quotations.

findings.claim: Flashcard 'What three pressures broke the armistice deadlock in 1953?' with a three-item list answer.
findings.truth: Question and answer rewritten around the June 1953 prisoner compromise, one idea.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: no list answers.

findings.claim: 'Do not stray into provenance or own knowledge ... Examiner reports flag bias-only commentary as a low-band trap.'
findings.truth: The 4-mark question requires contextual knowledge, and the examiner-report claim is invented. Tip rewritten.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B question 1.

findings.claim: (lessons 6, 7) 'In 1954 Eisenhower himself acknowledged privately that Ho would have won perhaps 80 percent of any free vote', repeated inside a composed July 1954 State Department source and in two flashcards.
findings.truth: The 80 per cent remark comes from Eisenhower's later published account of the period, not from a private acknowledgement made in 1954, and it compared Ho with Bao Dai. Content reworded to 'later acknowledged'; the anachronistic line inside the source replaced; both flashcards reworded.
findings.evidence: Eisenhower, 'Mandate for Change' (1963); the claim could not be sourced to any 1954 document.

findings.claim: 'the official result claimed he had secured 98.2% of the vote in Saigon, a city of 450,000 voters where 605,000 ballots were counted'.
findings.truth: The 98%+ figure was the national result. The Saigon anomaly was 605,025 votes counted against about 450,000 registered voters. The sentence conflated the two.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1955 State of Vietnam referendum' (605,025 votes in Saigon, 450,000 registered).

findings.claim: 'Examiners flag this distinction often.'
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; replaced with 'This distinction matters.'
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented exam claims.

findings.claim: (lessons 7, 8, 11, 13) Four more bare-list flashcard answers (Vietcong aims; why Strategic Hamlets failed; what Johnson announced on 31 March 1968; the four signatories of the Paris Accords).
findings.truth: Questions and answers rewritten so each card carries one idea.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: no list answers.

findings.claim: 'examiners want all three of content, provenance and your own contextual knowledge'.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; reworded as a statement about the question.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented exam claims.

findings.claim: (lessons 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13) Nine further 4-mark questions use 'Using Source X, identify two reasons/ways/claims/judgements/purposes ...'.
findings.truth: Converted to the 'How do you know? Explain your answer using Source X and your contextual knowledge' form, with mark schemes rebuilt to credit contextual knowledge.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B question 1.

findings.claim: (lessons 8, 9, 10, 11, 13) Composed sources carry invented archival provenance: 'drawn from the Public Papers of the Presidents', 'the Pentagon Papers', 'the Foreign Relations of the United States series', 'declassified CIA records', 'declassified court-martial records', 'the records of the 23rd Infantry Division', 'the CBS News archive', 'declassified White House records'.
findings.truth: Every archive tail stripped. The wording of these sources is composed, so no archive can be cited for it.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: strip invented archive provenances from composed practice sources.

findings.claim: (lessons 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13) Six more '16 marks - Source-Based Essay' questions ('Write an essay on the question ... Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim').
findings.truth: Converted to the statement essay with rebuilt mark schemes, each carrying the SPaG line.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B question 4.

findings.claim: (lessons 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13) Six questions typed '8 marks - Source Evaluation' ('Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian ...').
findings.truth: There is no 8-mark source question on this paper: the source questions are worth 4 and 12 marks and the 8-mark question is the narrative account. Each converted to a 4-mark source question on the same source, keeping the material.
findings.evidence: Spec assessment structure, Section B questions 1-3.

findings.claim: Match answer: Ho Chi Minh = 'Symbolic leader of communist North Vietnam'.
findings.truth: Ho was the actual leader of North Vietnam through this period, not a figurehead. Changed to 'Communist leader of North Vietnam from 1954'.
findings.evidence: Spec part two names Ho Chi Minh among the key individuals.

findings.claim: (lessons 9, 11) 'examiner reports flag ... as the typical mid-band ceiling' and 'examiner reports flag a common trap'.
findings.truth: Invented exam claims; both reworded.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented exam claims.

findings.claim: Source A is 'An extract from a New Yorker magazine article by journalist Seymour Hersh, published 20 November 1969'.
findings.truth: Hersh broke the My Lai story on 13 November 1969 through the Dispatch News Service, carried by about 35 newspapers. The lesson's own conclusion and flashcards say 'syndicated newspapers', so the source contradicted the lesson.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'My Lai massacre': 'My Lai was first revealed to the public on 13 November 1969 ... when Hersh published a story through the Dispatch News Service'.

findings.claim: The Ben Tre line quoted as 'it became necessary to destroy the village to save it'.
findings.truth: The reported line refers to a town, and the same sentence calls Ben Tre a town.
findings.evidence: Internal inconsistency; the standard reported wording uses 'town'.

findings.claim: Cronkite quoted as 'the only realistic, if unsatisfactory, conclusion'.
findings.truth: He said 'the only realistic, yet unsatisfactory, conclusion'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Walter Cronkite', 27 February 1968 closing editorial.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: 'high credibility because the North had no incentive to be honest about its losses to itself unless honest analysis was needed'.
findings.truth: Garbled and unusable as guidance; rewritten.
findings.evidence: Readability of a mark scheme students are shown.

findings.claim: (lessons 12, 13) 'Five million hectares of forest were defoliated' (L12) and 'Roughly 5 million hectares of forest had been defoliated' (L13).
findings.truth: About 7.7 million acres - 3.1 million hectares - of forest were defoliated. Five million is the acreage figure read as hectares.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Agent Orange': '7,700,000 acres (3,100,000 ha) ... of tropical forest were defoliated'.

findings.claim: 'fellow student Mary Ann Vecchio screaming over a body' at Kent State.
findings.truth: Vecchio was a 14-year-old runaway from Florida, not a Kent State student.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kent State shootings': 'a 14-year-old runaway, Mary Ann Vecchio'.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: 'June 1970: Congress repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution'.
findings.truth: The Senate voted to repeal in June 1970 and passed the Cooper-Church Amendment; the repeal itself took effect in January 1971.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Gulf of Tonkin Resolution' (Senate vote 24 June 1970; repeal enacted January 1971).

findings.claim: Source B: 'Moscow now competes for American friendship rather than for it.'
findings.truth: Meaningless as written; rewritten as 'Moscow must now compete for American friendship rather than count on it.'
findings.evidence: Readability of a source students must interpret.

findings.claim: 'Nixon's Secretary of State Henry Kissinger' (content), 'a private memo from Secretary of State to President in October 1972' (mark scheme), 'US Secretary of State who signed the 1973 Accords' (knowledge check) and 'Henry Kissinger, Nixon's Secretary of State' (flashcard).
findings.truth: Kissinger was National Security Adviser until 22 September 1973. He negotiated and signed the Paris Accords in that role. Lesson 12 of the same unit calls him National Security Adviser correctly, so the unit contradicted itself. All four corrected.
findings.evidence: Spec part three names 'the role of Kissinger'; Wikipedia 'Henry Kissinger' (Secretary of State from September 1973).

findings.claim: 'Hanoi launched the Ho Chi Minh Campaign in March 1975' (content and mark scheme).
findings.truth: The March 1975 attack in the Central Highlands was a separate campaign; the Ho Chi Minh Campaign was the final drive on Saigon from late April.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia '1975 Spring Offensive' / 'Ho Chi Minh Campaign'.

findings.claim: 'North Vietnamese tank 843 crashed through the gates of the Independence Palace' (twice in content, once in a mark scheme, once in a flashcard).
findings.truth: Accounts differ over which tank broke the main gate: 843 stalled at a side gate and its commander raised the flag, while 390 is credited with the main gate. The verifiable statement names no number.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Independence Palace': 'a tank of the North Vietnamese army bulldozed through the main gate' - no number given.

findings.claim: Source G, a November 1982 dedication speech, says 'On this wall are the names of 58,272 men and women.'
findings.truth: The wall carried 57,939 names at its dedication in 1982; the total only rose past 58,000 in later decades. The 1982 speech quoted a number that did not yet exist.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Vietnam Veterans Memorial': 'originally numbering 57,939 when it was dedicated in 1982'.

findings.claim: 'The Joint Chiefs warned the operation could turn into a disaster - one called it a 5,000-to-one shot.'
findings.truth: The 5,000-to-1 line is normally MacArthur's own, spoken at the August 1950 briefing to argue that he would take those odds; here it is put in the mouth of an unnamed Joint Chief, which reverses its meaning. I could not confirm the attribution from an available source this session. Options: (a) reassign it to MacArthur as his own argument, or (b) drop the quotation and keep 'The Joint Chiefs warned the operation could turn into a disaster.' I recommend (b) as the safe fix.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Battle of Inchon' does not contain the phrase; no verification obtained.

findings.claim: '600,000 Chinese' soldiers killed in Korea, stated as fact alongside the other casualty figures.
findings.truth: 600,000 is the high end of Western estimates. China's official figure is about 197,000 military deaths, and published estimates span roughly 200,000 to 600,000. Options: (a) keep 600,000 as the common Western estimate, or (b) write 'estimates of Chinese dead range from about 200,000 to 600,000'. I recommend (b), since the lesson presents every other figure as settled.
findings.evidence: Range of published estimates; no single authoritative value.

findings.claim: 'over four million students at 900 campuses walked out' (repeated in the key fact, a flashcard and two mark schemes).
findings.truth: The four-million figure is solid. The campus figure is not: the walk-outs are usually given as more than 450 campuses, while the ~900 figure refers to institutions that closed. Options: (a) change 900 to 'more than 450 campuses', or (b) keep 900 but attach it to closures. I recommend (a) in the content and (b) nowhere, since five places would need to agree.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Kent State shootings': 'more than 4 million students participated in organized walk-outs ... more than 450 campuses'.

findings.claim: 'Stalin's green light for invasion after eighteen months of lobbying'.
findings.truth: Kim first asked Stalin in March 1949 and was approved in the spring of 1950, so roughly twelve to thirteen months.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Korean War' chronology.

findings.claim: 'Truman's approval rating dropped to 22 percent' after MacArthur's dismissal.
findings.truth: Gallup's 22 per cent low for Truman is usually dated February 1952; polling shortly after the April 1951 dismissal is generally given in the mid-20s. Could not verify this session.
findings.evidence: No verification obtained.

findings.claim: 'Around 60% of those prisoners died in captivity' at Dien Bien Phu.
findings.truth: Of about 11,700 prisoners, roughly 3,300 were repatriated four months later, which is nearer 70 per cent lost.
findings.evidence: Standard accounts of the post-Dien Bien Phu prisoner columns; figures vary.

findings.claim: 'peaking at 540,000 in 1968'.
findings.truth: The recorded peak was about 543,400 in April 1969; end-1968 stood at about 536,100. 540,000 in 1968 is the standard textbook rounding and is left as it is.
findings.evidence: US Department of Defense troop-strength series.

findings.claim: (unit-wide) Almost every practice source in the unit is composed rather than a genuine document, including private letters, cables, memoirs and press dispatches.
findings.truth: The composed sources are pedagogically sound and are now free of invented archive claims and invented named-historian quotations. Recording it so the unit is not later mistaken for a set of real documents. Four sources are genuine or near-genuine and were checked: Eisenhower's 7 April 1954 domino remarks, Johnson's 4 August 1964 address, Cronkite's 27 February 1968 editorial and Nixon's 23 January 1973 address.
findings.evidence: Checker brief: label composed sources as a NOTE.

summary: Every lesson carried at least one finding. The dominant problem was exam-form drift: 45 of the 78 practice questions were set in forms this paper does not use (12 source-based 16-mark essays, 6 eight-mark source evaluations, 21 'identify two reasons' four-markers, 27 'construct a chronological explanation' stems), and nine exam tips described the wrong question or cited invented examiner reports. Factually the unit was strong; the substantive errors were Kissinger titled Secretary of State in 1972-73, Hersh's My Lai story ascribed to the New Yorker, an invented quotation ascribed to a named historian's real book, Rhee campaigning for independence 'from the United States', Mary Ann Vecchio called a Kent State student, and an acres-for-hectares slip on Agent Orange repeated in two lessons.
